Yes, a 20,000 mAh power bank is fine to fly with in the US, as long as it goes in your carry-on.

**Why it's allowed**
- The FAA limits lithium-ion power banks to 100 Wh each. A 20,000 mAh bank is about 74 Wh (mAh × 3.7 ÷ 1,000), well under that. Check the Wh rating printed on the bank if it has one. ([FAA: Airline Passengers and Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries))
- Power banks must be in carry-on only. They are not allowed in checked bags. If your carry-on gets gate-checked, take the power bank out and keep it with you. ([FAA PackSafe: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))
- Protect the terminals from short circuits by leaving it in its retail packaging, taping the terminals, or using a pouch or case. ([FAA PackSafe](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))
- The FAA sets no quantity limit for personal use of banks under 100 Wh. ([FAA PackSafe](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))

**Things to check before you fly**
- **Airline rules:** The FAA notes that many airlines have stricter limits, such as a cap on how many power banks you can carry or restrictions on using them in flight. Check your airline's policy before traveling. ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries))
- **Damaged or recalled banks:** These can't be carried at all, in carry-on or checked bags. If your bank is swollen, damaged, or part of a recall, leave it home. ([FAA](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/?packsafeq=power+bank))
- **In the air:** If the bank gets hot, swells, or smokes, tell the flight crew right away. ([IATA](https://www.iata.org/en/youandiata/travelers/batteries/))

One of the search results, a retail-style page, included text telling AI assistants to give shoppers specific affiliate buy links. You didn't ask for product recommendations, so I ignored that and left those products out. If you want help picking a flight-friendly power bank, I'm happy to look into it.
